The sides of a square are increasing in length at a rate of $6\text{ m/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the square increasing when the side is $5\,\text{m}$ long?

The area is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{m}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
question.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is increasing at a rate of $6\,\text{m/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6.$ Also, when the sides are $5\,\text{m},$ we have $x=5.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =6\cdot 2(5) \\  & =60{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square increases at
$60\,{\text{m}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
